title: Raising Lazarus
overview: John 11 narrates the profound event of Jesus raising Lazarus from the dead, a pivotal miracle that reveals Jesus' authority over life and death and His identity as the resurrection and the life. The chapter begins with Lazarus’ illness and Jesus’ deliberate delay in going to him, highlighting divine purpose in suffering. The grief of Mary and Martha contrasts with Jesus’ assurance of resurrection, culminating in the dramatic resurrection itself. This miracle intensifies opposition against Jesus, leading to the religious leaders’ plot to kill Him. The chapter powerfully illustrates Jesus’ compassion, divine power, and the call to faith in Him as the source of eternal life.
structure:
**Verses 1-16: The Illness and Jesus’ Delay.** The chapter opens with Lazarus’ sickness and Jesus’ intentional delay, emphasizing that the sickness serves to glorify God and reveal Jesus’ divine power. The disciples express concern about returning to Judea, but Jesus speaks of spiritual light and prepares them for Lazarus’ death.

**Verses 17-37: The Arrival and Mourning.** Jesus arrives after Lazarus has been dead four days. Martha and Mary express their grief and faith, while Jesus shows deep compassion, weeping alongside them and the mourners.

**Verses 38-44: The Resurrection of Lazarus.** Jesus commands the stone to be removed and calls Lazarus forth from the tomb, demonstrating His power over death and affirming faith in Him.

**Verses 45-57: The Aftermath and Plot Against Jesus.** Many believe in Jesus after witnessing the miracle, but the religious leaders convene to plot His death, fearing the loss of their authority and the nation’s stability. Jesus withdraws to a secluded place, anticipating the coming Passover and His ultimate sacrifice.

keyVerses.text: Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:
keyVerses.significance: This verse encapsulates the core theological truth of the chapter: Jesus’ identity as the source of resurrection and eternal life. It offers believers assurance of life beyond physical death through faith in Him.
The shortest verse in the Bible reveals Jesus’ genuine humanity and compassion. His sorrow over Lazarus’ death shows His empathy with human grief, deepening the understanding of His incarnate love.

keyVerses.text: When Jesus heard that, he said, This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby .
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights the divine purpose behind Lazarus’ illness, framing suffering as an opportunity for God’s glory and Jesus’ revelation as the Son of God.

keyVerses.text: And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth. And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go.
keyVerses.significance: These verses depict the miraculous resurrection, demonstrating Jesus’ power over death and inviting believers to freedom through Him.

characters.name: Jesus Christ
characters.description: The Son of God who demonstrates divine authority over death by raising Lazarus. He reveals His identity as the resurrection and the life, shows deep compassion, and prepares His followers for His own death.

characters.name: Lazarus
characters.description: Brother of Mary and Martha, whose death and resurrection serve as the central miracle of the chapter, illustrating Jesus’ power and the promise of eternal life.

characters.name: Martha
characters.description: Sister of Lazarus who expresses faith in Jesus’ power to heal and resurrection, engaging in theological dialogue with Jesus about life after death.

characters.name: Mary
characters.description: Sister of Lazarus who mourns deeply and demonstrates faith by seeking Jesus, highlighting the personal and emotional impact of Jesus’ ministry.

characters.name: Religious Leaders (Pharisees and Chief Priests)
characters.description: Opponents of Jesus who respond to the miracle with fear and conspiracy, plotting His death to preserve their authority and political stability.

themes.description: The chapter centers on Jesus’ power to give life beyond physical death, affirming the Christian hope of resurrection through faith in Christ.
Martha’s confession and Jesus’ question to her emphasize belief in Jesus as the Messiah and Son of God, a key to receiving eternal life.
Jesus’ delay and the sickness itself serve to glorify God, showing that trials can reveal God’s power and purpose.
Jesus’ weeping and emotional response demonstrate His genuine empathy and love for humanity.

themes.theme: Conflict Between Jesus and Religious Authorities
themes.description: The miracle intensifies opposition, illustrating the spiritual battle between God’s kingdom and worldly powers.

historicalContext: John 11 is set in first-century Judea, near Jerusalem, during the time of Roman occupation. Bethany, the village of Lazarus, Mary, and Martha, was a small community about two miles from Jerusalem, making it a frequent place for Jesus to visit. The Jewish customs of mourning and burial are evident, including the four-day period after death, which was believed to confirm death beyond doubt. The religious leaders, including Pharisees and chief priests, held significant influence but were under Roman political control, leading to tensions over Jesus’ growing popularity and miracles. The Passover festival, approaching at the chapter’s end, heightened political and religious sensitivities, setting the stage for the escalating conflict.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This perspective emphasizes Jesus’ sovereignty over life and death, viewing Lazarus’ resurrection as a sign of the final resurrection of believers. It highlights faith in Christ as essential for eternal life and sees the chapter as revealing God’s glory through Jesus’ obedient suffering.

Catholic theology focuses on the sacramental implications of Jesus as the resurrection and life, connecting this miracle to baptism and the hope of resurrection. It also stresses Jesus’ compassion and the call to trust in God’s providence amid suffering.

Evangelicals stress personal faith in Jesus as the risen Lord, underscoring the chapter’s call to believe in Him for eternal life. The miracle is seen as a powerful testimony to Jesus’ divinity and a call to repentance and trust.

crossReferences.connection: Paul’s teaching on Christ as the firstfruits of resurrection parallels Jesus’ raising of Lazarus as a foretaste of eternal life.
The prophecy of God swallowing up death forever is fulfilled in Jesus’ power over death demonstrated in this chapter.
Paul’s explanation of baptism into Christ’s death and resurrection connects to the new life Jesus offers, as shown in Lazarus’ resurrection.
The preciousness of the death of God’s saints is reflected in the mourning and Jesus’ compassion over Lazarus.
Jesus’ victory over death and the devil is illustrated in His raising of Lazarus, freeing believers from the fear of death.

application: Trust in Jesus’ timing and sovereignty, even when answers to prayer seem delayed.
Believe in Jesus as the resurrection and the life, anchoring hope beyond physical death.
Emulate Jesus’ compassion by comforting those who mourn and suffer.
Stand firm in faith despite opposition or fear, following Thomas’ example of commitment.
Use trials and suffering as opportunities to witness God’s glory to others.
Respond to Jesus’ call promptly, like Mary, demonstrating active faith.
conclusion: John 11 powerfully reveals Jesus’ divine authority over death and His compassionate heart toward human suffering. Through the raising of Lazarus, believers are called to place their faith in Jesus as the resurrection and the life, assured of eternal life beyond physical death. The chapter also warns of the spiritual opposition that faith may provoke, encouraging steadfastness and trust in God’s sovereign plan. Its enduring message invites Christians to witness God’s glory through trials and to embrace the hope found only in Christ.
timeline: c. AD 30-33 - Ministry of Jesus in Judea

definitions.definition: A biblical euphemism for death, used by Jesus to describe Lazarus’ state before resurrection.
The manifestation of God’s presence, power, and holiness, often revealed through miraculous acts.
The act of rising from the dead to eternal life, central to Christian faith and Jesus’ identity.
A cloth used to wrap the face of the deceased in burial customs of the time.
A Jewish religious sect known for strict adherence to the Law and traditions, often opposing Jesus.

outline.heading: The Sickness and Divine Purpose
outline.description: Introduction of Lazarus’ illness, Jesus’ delay, and teaching on spiritual light and death as sleep, setting the stage for the miracle.

outline.heading: Jesus’ Arrival and the Sisters’ Faith
outline.description: Jesus meets Martha and Mary, engages in theological dialogue about resurrection, and expresses deep compassion through weeping.

outline.heading: The Resurrection Miracle
outline.description: Jesus commands the stone’s removal and calls Lazarus forth, demonstrating His power over death and inviting faith.

outline.heading: Reaction and Plot Against Jesus
outline.description: Many believe in Jesus, but religious leaders conspire to kill Him, escalating the conflict that leads to the Passion.
